statement: In sleep-laboratory studies of cannabis products taken by mouth, sleep did not detectably change on average: in six modern trials pooled in a 2025 meta-analysis (Velzeboer et al., 2025; AMSTAR 2 critically low; 178 participants, editors' sum from Table 1), mostly of CBD or low-dose THC medicines and four of six in people with sleep disorders (sleep apnea, insomnia, REM behaviour disorder in Parkinson's disease), total sleep time (standardized difference -0.02, 95% CI -0.25 to 0.21), time to fall asleep, waking during the night, sleep efficiency and deep sleep did not differ from placebo or baseline, while results for REM (dream) sleep were inconsistent (-0.04, -0.52 to 0.45; I-squared 77%). Small studies from 1972 to 1982, mostly with high oral THC doses, could not be pooled, and most of them found less REM sleep; and three comparisons (1973 to 2008) of people who smoke cannabis with people who do not mostly found no difference. All six pooled studies gave cannabis by mouth, and the authors note that clinical research has almost only studied oral use, so the result may not apply to smoked or vaped cannabis. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
plain: Many people use cannabis to help them sleep. In sleep labs, people who took cannabis products by mouth, mostly medicines with CBD or a little THC, slept about the same as when they took a dummy pill: no longer, no faster to fall asleep, no deeper. Dream sleep results did not agree. These studies did not test smoking or vaping, and most people in them had a sleep problem.
population: Adults in sleep-laboratory studies, mostly people with sleep apnea, insomnia or REM behaviour disorder with Parkinson's disease, and some healthy volunteers
exposure: Cannabis products taken by mouth (THC, dronabinol, CBD or combinations; doses are study conditions in the study card)
comparator: Placebo or the same people's baseline nights
outcome: Polysomnographic sleep: total sleep time, time to fall asleep, waking after sleep onset, sleep efficiency, sleep stages, REM sleep
magnitude: Pooled standardized mean differences (95% CI), as printed in the forest plots: total sleep time -0.02 (-0.25 to 0.21); sleep onset latency -0.06 (-0.28 to 0.17); wake after sleep onset 0.11 (-0.13 to 0.34); sleep efficiency 0.01 (-0.25 to 0.27); slow-wave sleep 0.14 (-0.07 to 0.35); REM -0.04 (-0.52 to 0.45), I-squared 77.5%; REM latency -0.03 (-0.56 to 0.50), I-squared 76.1%.

evidence.extracted: Administration meta-analyses: total sleep time -0.02 (-0.25 to 0.21), 4 studies (5 arms), I-squared 0%; sleep onset latency -0.06 (-0.28 to 0.17), 5 studies, 0%; wake after sleep onset 0.11 (-0.13 to 0.34), 0%; sleep efficiency 0.01 (-0.25 to 0.27), 0%. Of 12 administration studies measuring total sleep time, one (n = 4) found an increase; of 12 measuring onset latency, one (n = 2) found an increase. The text prints +0.021, +0.056 and -0.009 for three of these, with intervals centred on the figures' values.
evidence.source_read: PDF PDFs/Cannabis/Velzeboer_2025_SleepArchitectureMA.pdf (published version; forest plots read on rendered pages)

evidence.extracted: Stages: N1 0.15 (-0.07 to 0.37); N2 0.01 (-0.21 to 0.23); slow-wave sleep 0.14 (-0.07 to 0.35); REM -0.04 (-0.52 to 0.45), I-squared 77.5%, with both arms of one dronabinol trial in sleep apnea raising REM (1.16 and 0.72) and CBD in REM behaviour disorder lowering it (-0.98); REM latency -0.03 (-0.56 to 0.50), I-squared 76.1%. Of 14 administration studies, six found less REM sleep and one more.
evidence.source_read: PDF PDFs/Cannabis/Velzeboer_2025_SleepArchitectureMA.pdf (published version; forest plots read on rendered pages)

evidence.locator: Table 1, administration rows (p. 4); Results 3.1.1 (pp. 6-7) and 3.1.5 (p. 9); Discussion, paragraph on early REM studies (p. 12) and on oral versus inhaled use (p. 13, left column)
evidence.extracted: The six pooled administration studies were all oral: THC with or without CBD in 8 healthy volunteers, dronabinol in sleep apnea (15 and 73 people), CBD in 26 healthy volunteers and in people with REM behaviour disorder and Parkinson's disease (17 and 16 in two arms), and a THC, CBN and CBD product in 23 people with insomnia. Early 1972-1982 studies (2 to 11 people, mostly high THC doses) lacked data for pooling; most reported less REM sleep. The authors note the clinical literature almost exclusively studies oral use, not inhalation.

evidence.locator: Table 1, chronic use rows (p. 4); Results 3.2.1 (p. 10, left column) and 3.2.7-3.2.8 (p. 11)
evidence.extracted: Three comparisons of people who use cannabis with people who do not (inhaled cannabis, 1973-2008) found no significant differences in most sleep measures; one found shorter total sleep time and less slow-wave sleep, and one more REM sleep.

risk_of_bias.note: Mostly randomized trials rated low risk by the review, but one non-randomized study is pooled with them, the handling of crossover designs is not described, and the review is AMSTAR 2 critically low with sign errors in its text.

inconsistency.note: Sleep time, onset, waking and efficiency consistent (I-squared 0-6%); REM inconsistent, which the statement says.

indirectness.note: CBD and THC products and different patient groups are combined in single pools; oral medicinal products only.

imprecision.note: 178 participants; intervals of about plus or minus 0.25 standard deviations cannot exclude small effects, and REM intervals are wide.

publication_bias.note: Not assessed (too few studies); not downgraded separately.

grade.reasoning: Randomized evidence starts high; risk of bias, indirectness and imprecision each -1 give very low. Status replicated: the modern trials agree in showing no change in sleep duration, onset or efficiency. The relation is worded as no detectable change for these products and populations, not as proof of no effect, and does not extend to smoked or vaped cannabis.
